source_text: ΟΜΙΛΙΑ ΚΑʹ. Περὶ τοῦ μὴ προσηλῶσθαι τοῖς βιωτικοῖς, καὶ περὶ τοῦ γενομένου ἐμπρησμοῦ ἔξωθεν τῆς Ἐκκλησίας. Ἐγὼ μὲν ᾤμην, ἀγαπητοὶ, σφοδρότερον ἑκάστοτε τοῦ λόγου τὸ κέντρον προσάγων, λυπηρός τις εἶναι δόξειν ὑμῖν, ὡς περιττήν τινα παῤῥησίαν ἐπιδεικνύ μενος, καὶ οὔτε ξένῳ πρέπουσαν, οὔτε ἀνδρὶ κατειλημ μένῳ παραπλησίοις ἐγκλήμασιν· ὑμεῖς δὲ ἐκ τῶν ἐλέγχων εἰς εὔνοιαν ἠρεθίσθητε, καὶ τὰς ἀπὸ τῆς γλώττης πληγὰς ὑπέκκαυμα πόθου πεποίησθε πλείονος. Καὶ οὐδὲν ξένον. Ἐστὲ γὰρ σοφοὶ τὰ τοῦ πνεύματος. Ἔλεγχε δὲ σοφὸν, καὶ ἀγαπήσει σε, φησί που τῶν αὑτοῦ λόγων ὁ Σολομών. Διὰ τοῦτο, ἀδελφοὶ, καὶ νῦν ἐπὶ τὴν αὐτὴν ἥκω παραίνεσιν, ὅπηπερ ἂν οἷός τε ὦ, τῶν τοῦ διαβόλου δικτύων ὑμᾶς ἀπάγειν βουλόμενος. Πολὺν γὰρ, ἀγαπητοὶ, καὶ ποικίλον ἐφ' ἡμέραν ἡμῖν ὁ τῆς ἀληθείας ἐχθρὸς προσάγει τὸν πόλεμον. Προσάγει δὲ, ὡς ἴστε, τὰς ἡμετέρας ἐπιθυμίας καθ' ἡμῶν βέλη ποιούμενος, καὶ παρ' ἡμῶν εἰς τὸ βλάπτειν ἡμᾶς ἀεὶ λαμβάνων ἰσχύν. Ἐπειδὴ γὰρ τὸ πολὺ τῆς ἐκείνου δυνάμεως ὁ Δεσπότης νόμοις ἀλύτοις κατέδησε, καὶ οὐκ εἴασεν εἰς ἅπαξ ὁρμήσαντα τὸ γένος ἐκτρῖψαι τῆς γῆς, κλέπτει τὴν καθ' ἡμῶν νίκην λοιπὸν ἐκ τῆς ἡμετέρας ἀνοίας ὁ βάσκανος. Καὶ καθάπερ οἱ πονηροὶ καὶ πλεονε κτικοὶ τῶν ἀνθρώπων, οἷς ἔργον μέν ἐστι καὶ προαί ρεσις ἐκ τῶν ἀλλοτρίων πλουτεῖν, δύναμις δὲ οὐ πάρ εστιν ὥστε μετὰ παῤῥησίας βιάζεσθαι, ταῖς ὁδοῖς ἐφεδρεύειν εἰώθασι· καὶ εἰ ἴδωσί τι χωρίον περὶ αὐ τὰς, ἢ φάραγξι βαθείαις διεῤῥωγὸς, ἢ φυτῶν πυκνότητι σύσκιον, εἰς τοῦτο καταδυόμενοι, καὶ τὴν ἐκ πολλοῦ πρόοψιν τῶν ὁδοιπορούντων τοιούτοις ὑποτεμνόμενοι προκαλύμμασιν, ἀθρόον ἐπιπηδῶσιν αὐτοῖς, ὥστε μὴ πρότερον δυνηθῆναί τινα τοὺς τοῦ κινδύνου βρόχους ἰδεῖν πρὶν εἰς τούτους πεσεῖν· οὕτως ὁ δυσ μενὴς ἄνωθεν ἡμῖν καὶ πολέμιος τὰς τῶν κοσμι κῶν τέρψεων ὑποτρέχων σκιὰς, αἳ περὶ τὴν ὁδὸν τοῦ βίου τούτου πεφύκασι δειναὶ κρῦψαι λῃστὴν, καὶ τὸν ἐπιβουλεύοντα ποιῆσαι λαθεῖν, ἐντεῦθεν ἀπροόπτως τὰς τῆς ἀπωλείας ὑποσπείρει παγίδας ἡμῖν. Δεῖ τοίνυν ἡμᾶς, εἴπερ ἐθέλοιμεν ἀσφαλῶς τὴν ὑπο κειμένην ὁδὸν τοῦ βίου διαδραμεῖν, καὶ παραστῆσαι Χριστῷ τὴν ψυχήν τε ὁμοῦ καὶ τὸ σῶμα τῆς ἐκ τῶν τραυμάτων αἰσχύνης ἐλεύθερα, καὶ τοὺς ἐπὶ τῇ νίκῃ στεφάνους λαβεῖν, ἐγρηγορότας περιάγειν ἀεὶ παντα χόσε τοὺς τῆς ψυχῆς ὀφθαλμοὺς καὶ πάντα ὑπο πιεύειν ὅσα τερπνὰ, καὶ παρατρέχειν εὐθὺς, καὶ μηδενὶ προσερείδειν τὴν ἔννοιαν, μηδὲ εἰ χρυσὸς φαίνοιτο χύδην προκείμενος, ἕτοιμος εἰς τὰς τῶν βουλομένων χεῖρας ἐλθεῖν (Πλοῦτος γὰρ, φησὶν, ἐὰν ῥέῃ, μὴ προστίθεσθε καρδίᾳ)· μηδὲ εἰ γῆ βλαστάνουσα πᾶσαν τρυφὴν, καὶ πολυτελεῖς δεικνύουσα σκηνὰς (Ἡμῶν γὰρ τὸ πολίτευμα ἐν οὐ ρανῷ, ἐξ οὗ καὶ Σωτῆρα ἀπεκδεχόμεθα Χριστόν)· μηδὲ εἰ χορεῖαι, καὶ κῶμοι, καὶ μέθαι, καὶ καταυλού μεναι τράπεζαι (Ματαιότης γὰρ, φησὶν, ματαιοτήτων, τὰ πάντα ματαιότης)· μηδὲ εἰ σωμάτων κάλλη προτείνοιτο, παρὰ πονηρῶν ψυχῶν ἐνοικούμενα (Ἀπὸ προσώπου γὰρ γυναικὸς ὡς ἀπὸ προσώπου ὄφεως φεῦγε, φησὶν ὁ Σοφός)· μηδὲ εἰ δυναστεῖαι καὶ τυραννίδες, καὶ δορυφόρων ἢ κολάκων ἐσμοί· μηδὲ εἰ θρόνος ὑψηλὸς καὶ λαμπρὸς, ὑποζεύξας ἔθνη καὶ πόλεις εἰς δουλείαν ἑκούσιον (Πᾶσα γὰρ σὰρξ ὡς χόρτος, καὶ πᾶσα δόξα ἀνθρώπου ὡς ἄνθος χόρτου· ἐξηράνθη ὁ χόρτος, καὶ τὸ ἄν θος ἐξέπεσε).
thought_title: The devil ambushes the road of life through worldly pleasures
orientation: Basil opens his homily by explaining that the devil, unable to destroy humanity outright, ambushes people on the road of life through deceptive worldly pleasures.
pass_a_gloss: Homily 21. On not clinging to worldly things, and on the fire that happened outside the church. I for my part was thinking, beloved, that by applying the sting of the word more sharply each time, I would seem to be somewhat painful to you, as one displaying a certain excessive frankness, and one fitting neither for a stranger nor for a man caught in similar accusations; but you were stirred from the reproofs to goodwill, and you made the blows from the tongue a kindling of greater longing. And nothing strange. For you are wise in the things of the spirit. Reprove a wise man, and he will love you, says Solomon somewhere in his words. For this reason, brothers, I have now come to the same exhortation, wishing, so far as I may be able, to lead you away from the nets of the devil. For the enemy of truth brings against us, beloved, a great and varied war day by day. And he brings it, as you know, making our own desires into arrows against us, and always taking from us strength to harm us. For since the Master bound the greater part of that one's power with unbreakable laws, and did not allow him, having rushed at once, to wipe out the race of the earth, the envious one steals the victory over us henceforth from our own folly. And just as the wicked and greedy among men, whose work and choice it is to grow rich from the things of others, but who do not have power to use force with boldness, are accustomed to lie in wait on the roads; and if they see some spot around them, either broken by deep ravines, or shaded by the density of plants, sinking down into this, and cutting off the long-range view of the travelers with such coverings, they leap upon them all at once, so that no one is able to see the snares of the danger before falling into them; so the hostile one and enemy from above, running beneath the shadows of worldly delights, which have grown around the road of this life, terrible to hide a robber, and to make the plotter escape notice, from there sows for us unforeseen the traps of destruction. Therefore we must, if we wish to run safely the road of life that lies before us, and to present to Christ the soul together with the body free from the shame of wounds, and to receive the crowns of victory, keep the eyes of the soul always awake and turned in every direction, and suspect everything pleasant, and run past it immediately, and fix the thought on nothing, not even if gold should appear poured out in heaps, ready to come into the hands of those who wish it (For if wealth flows, it says, do not set your heart on it); not even if the earth should sprout every luxury, and display costly tents (For our citizenship is in heaven, from which also we await a Savior, Christ); not even if dances, and revels, and drunkenness, and tables accompanied by flutes (For vanity of vanities, it says, all things are vanity); not even if beauties of bodies should be offered, inhabited by wicked souls (For from the face of a woman as from the face of a snake flee, says the Wise One); not even if powers and tyrannies, and swarms of bodyguards or flatterers; not even if a throne high and bright, having yoked nations and cities into willing slavery (For all flesh is as grass, and all glory of man as the flower of grass; the grass withered, and the flower fell).

The glossary mandates 'road' for ὁδός, the controlling image of the homily.

pass_b_english: I thought, beloved, that by pressing the sting of my words harder each time I would seem harsh to you—as though I were putting on a display of boldness that was excessive, and fitting neither for a stranger nor for a man caught up in similar accusations. But you have been stirred by my reproofs toward goodwill, and you have made the blows from my tongue into kindling for a greater longing. And that is no surprise, for you are wise in the things of the Spirit. “Reprove a wise man, and he will love you,” says Solomon somewhere in his words (Proverbs 9:8).

For this reason, brothers and sisters, I have come now to the same exhortation, wanting, as far as I am able, to draw you away from the nets of the devil. For the enemy of truth wages a great and varied war against us every day, beloved. And he wages it, as you know, by making our own desires into arrows against us, always drawing from us the strength to harm us. For since the Master bound most of that enemy’s power with unbreakable laws and did not permit him to rush in all at once and wipe out the race of the earth, the envious one now steals his victory over us from our own folly.

Just as wicked and greedy people—whose work and deliberate choice it is to grow rich from what belongs to others, but who lack the power to use open force—are accustomed to lie in wait along the roads; and if they see a spot beside them, either broken by deep ravines or shaded by a thick growth of trees, they sink down into it, cutting off the travelers’ view from afar with such screens, and then leap on them all at once, so that no one can see the snares of danger before falling into them—so too our hostile enemy from above runs beneath the shadows of worldly pleasures. These shadows grow along the road of this life, and they are terrible at hiding a robber and making the one who plots against us escape notice. From there he sows the traps of destruction for us unseen.

Therefore, if we want to run safely along the road of life that lies before us, and to present to Christ our soul and body together free from the shame of wounds, and to receive the crowns of victory, we must always keep the eyes of the soul awake and turning in every direction. We must be wary of everything pleasant and run past it at once, fixing our mind on nothing—not even if gold appears poured out before us, ready to come into the hands of anyone who wants it. For Scripture says, “If wealth flows in, do not set your heart on it” (Psalm 62:10). Not even if the earth sprouts every luxury and displays costly tents, for “our citizenship is in heaven, from which we also await a Savior, Christ” (Philippians 3:20). Not even if there are dances and revels and drunkenness and tables accompanied by flutes, for “vanity of vanities,” it says, “all things are vanity” (Ecclesiastes 1:2). Not even if beautiful bodies are held out to you, inhabited by wicked souls, for “flee from a woman’s face as from the face of a serpent,” says the Wise One (Sirach 21:2). Not even if there are powers and tyrannies and swarms of bodyguards or flatterers. Not even if there is a high and shining throne that has yoked nations and cities into willing slavery, for “all flesh is like grass, and all human glory like the flower of grass; the grass withers, and the flower falls” (Isaiah 40:6-7).

refereed.quote: and fitting neither for a stranger nor for a man caught up in similar accusations
refereed.source_quote: καὶ οὔτε ξένῳ πρέπουσαν, οὔτε ἀνδρὶ κατειλημμένῳ παραπλησίοις ἐγκλήμασιν
refereed.why: The English omits the crucial word "similar" (παραπλησίοις). Basil says the boldness is unfitting for "a man caught up in similar accusations"—meaning Basil himself is under similar accusations as his hearers. The omission of "similar" loses the force that Basil identifies with his congregation's situation.
